title: What do McLaren’s newest upgrades tell us ahead of Monza?
excerpt:
On top of Hungary’s all-new floor, wakeboards and floor slots, McLaren brought to Zandvoort a new rear wing, engine cover, diffuser tweaks and new front wheel rims as further discrete performance items.

“The items aren’t linked as a package,” explained McLaren’s technical director Neil Houldey of the Zandvoort parts. “They all provide aero performance as individual components and don’t need each other to perform.”

This double hit of upgrades in consecutive races proved very powerful and helped Lando Norris to back-to-back Grand Prix victories, both of them from pole position.

title: Ferrari reveal special Schumacher-inspired livery for Monza
excerpt:
Ferrari have presented a special one-off livery for their home race at Monza, paying tribute to seven-time World Champion Michael Schumacher.

It is now 30 years since the German joined the Scuderia, and 20 years since his final victory with the team – scored at the 2006 Chinese Grand Prix.

As well as claiming five of his world titles with the Maranello-based squad, Schumacher bagged five Monza wins in red (in 1996, 1998, 2000, 2003 and 2006).

Heading into the weekend, Ferrari revealed bespoke race suits that will be worn by current drivers Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton, featuring Schumacher’s logo and the seven stars he used to carry on his helmet to signify his seven titles.

On Tuesday morning, the outfit followed up on those comments by showcasing a Schumacher-inspired car livery, again noting the details above around their usual 2026 design.

Ferrari explained that this week’s wide-ranging tributes are inspired by Schumacher’s “impact on the racing world” and “his enduring mindset”.

title: 7 memorable Italian Grand Prix moments from Monza
excerpt:
The Italian Grand Prix is only a few days away, and Monza is ready to welcome the teams, drivers and fans in typical Italian fashion. From teary moments to the Tifosi showing up in style, the fastest circuit in Formula 1 has never lacked entertainment on or off the track.

Monza was on the F1 calendar from the very beginning and has hosted all Italian Grands Prix but one since 1950. Here are some of the most unforgettable moments from the Temple of Speed in recent racing history...

Leclerc delights the Tifosi

There's arguably nothing more special for an F1 driver than winning for Ferrari on home soil at Monza – something Charles Leclerc acheived in 2019 when he topped the podium in Italy, taking his second career win in Formula 1 and his first at Monza.

“There were people as far as I could see,” he said afterwards. “It was packed. I was trying to find my mum. She was in a grandstand... I was trying to find her but there were way too many people.”

Schumacher equals Senna's tally

No driver has won more races for Ferrari than the great Michael Schumacher, but perhaps one of his most emotional victories was in the 2000 Italian Grand Prix?

After missing the previous year’s Grand Prix, the German driver returned to Monza in top shape, winning the race in front of the Tifosi. It was his 41st career victory, meaning he equalled the tally Ayrton Senna – something a very emotional Schumacher was reminded about in the post-race press conference.

Ferrari turns 90

Ferrari chose the weekend of the Italian Grand Prix to celebrate their 90th anniversary in 2019, when they took over Piazza Duomo in Milan to hold a special “90 years of emotions” event which saw Charles Leclerc and Sebastian Vettel alongside drivers and management from the past, marking the storied history of the Maranello team in front of a sea of red jerseys and caps with the iconic Duomo di Milano as a backdrop.

The Tifosi gather at the Piazza Duomo during the “90 Years of Emotion” event in 2019

A host of former Ferrari drivers were in attendance

Piazza Duomo was the setting for Ferrari's 90th year celebration

A maiden victory for Gasly

Monza without grandstands packed with passionate supporters is almost impossible to imagine. But in 2020 – due to the Covid pandemic – the Italian Grand Prix was held behind closed doors, and in an empty venue, Pierre Gasly found his way to success.

The French driver, wearing the colours of the other Italian team – then known as AlphaTauri – raced to his first ever Formula 1 victory.

Vettel's first triumph

But Gasly's win in 2020 wasn't the first time a driver from 'Italy's other team' had raced to a maiden victory at Monza.

Sebastian Vettel was in just his first full season as an F1 driver when he claimed a shock pole position for Toro Rosso at the Italian Grand Prix – and then followed that up with his first ever win.

The shoey returns

The Italian Grand Prix holds a special place in Daniel Ricciardo’s heart. The Australian won at Monza for McLaren in 2021, three years after his last victory. But it wasn’t a lucky win – Ricciardo led the race from start to finish and after a 1,204-day wait, he was back on the top of the podium ahead of his team mate Lando Norris, and Valtteri Bottas.

And what a better way to celebrate the long-awaited win with the iconic shoey celebration including Norris and McLaren boss Zak Brown?

Hamilton arriving in Monza in style

More recently, Sir Lewis Hamilton wanted to show up in style for his first Italian Grand Prix as a Ferrari driver – and he did not disappoint.

The seven-time world champion arrived at the circuit for last year's event riding a motorbike in the colours of the Italian flag.

He went on to finish sixth in that race, but will be hoping he can challenge for victory this weekend, after he took his first Grand Prix win in red earlier this year in Barcelona.

title: 5 storylines we’re excited about ahead of the Italian GP
excerpt:
The second half of the season is well and truly underway and the final two European rounds take place over a double-header that kicks off in Italy. With McLaren resurgent but plenty for the home fans to get excited about, there are sure to be a number of talking points when the paddock arrives in Monza.

Antonelli set for a home race penalty

Given the support Ferrari always receive at Monza, the Italian fans could find themselves slightly torn this weekend, as Kimi Antonelli arrives at his home race as the championship leader.

Rewind 12 months and it would have been a surprising prediction to suggest Antonelli would be 59 points clear in the standings in just his second season in Formula 1, even with the expectation that Mercedes would deliver a championship-contending car.

Yet as the Silver Arrows continue to prioritise the best approach to the season as a whole – rather than any individual race – Antonelli will face a tall order to secure victory in his home Grand Prix due to a planned power unit penalty.

Reliability issues mean Mercedes believe they won’t make it to the end of the season without taking a penalty with each car at some stage, and they also have the potential to upgrade the power unit through the FIA’s Advanced Development and Upgrade Opportunities (ADUO) mechanism.

Whether it is a new specification that is introduced at Monza or not, the team have confirmed Antonelli will take a full new power unit and start towards the back of the grid.

“With Kimi, we're taking the full thing,” Toto Wolff said in Zandvoort. “Our calculations say that that's the best track to take it. Obviously, algorithms don't take their nationality into consideration. We're here to fight for a championship and not get the most PR.”

Wolff confirms Antonelli is set for grid penalty at Monza

Red Bull’s driver situation

The summer shutdown ended with an unexpected driver line-up change – albeit only a temporary one – at Red Bull, after Isack Hadjar injured his wrist ahead of the Dutch Grand Prix, ruling him out of the race weekend at Zandvoort.

Liam Lawson was promoted in his place, and impressed despite the lack of practice mileage on offer during the Sprint weekend. By Saturday’s Qualifying session, Lawson was able to get close to Max Verstappen and secured a spot alongside his team mate on the fourth row, before a solid run to seventh place behind the McLaren, Mercedes and Ferrari cars.

With Lawson at Red Bull, Yuki Tsunoda returned at Racing Bulls and also had a strong weekend, just missing out on points. So both proved to be strong replacements while Hadjar recovers.

It has not yet been confirmed if Hadjar will be fit to return this weekend at Monza, but if not then it is expected that Red Bull will stick with the Zandvoort line-ups, giving both Lawson and Tsunoda another chance to impress. While it will be a race on a very different type of circuit, they would have three practice sessions to help them build on top of their previous weekend’s experience.

Stability in the driver market

In the build-up to the Dutch Grand Prix weekend, three driver contracts were confirmed that suggested there will be little movement across the grid in 2027.

First up was Alex Albon remaining with Williams, shortly followed by his team mate Carlos Sainz also committing his future to the team and ensuring an unchanged driver line-up for James Vowles to work with next year.

Then came the big news of Max Verstappen extending his Red Bull stay until at least the end of 2030, as the Dutchman reaffirmed his intention to complete his whole career with the team.

Since leaving the Netherlands, there has been further confirmation of a driver retaining their seat, as Franco Colapinto’s strong season has been rewarded with another year at Alpine alongside Pierre Gasly.

As it stands, there have only been extensions and renewals confirmed – with Lando Norris and McLaren also committing long-term to each other – as the driver market has stabilised this year. Aston Martin are a team of interest as Fernando Alonso has yet to announce his plans for 2027, while there could potentially be movement at Haas and Racing Bulls.

Ollie Bearman is expected to continue with Haas, and Esteban Ocon’s recent form shows he is doing everything he can to remain alongside him, but both seats are currently still available.

Although unconfirmed at this stage, it would be a major surprise if Isack Hadjar and Arvid Lindblad don’t keep their seats at Red Bull and Racing Bulls respectively, while Lawson’s substitute appearance keeps him in the mix for another season despite the emergence of Red Bull junior Nikola Tsolov.

Why Norris and McLaren have committed to each other for the long term

The Tifosi

Sure, Kimi Antonelli is leading the Drivers’ Championship, but you can still expect to see a sea of red at Monza as the Tifosi come out in force.

Although McLaren have won the past two races, Ferrari have been Mercedes’ closest challenger on average this season, with Lewis Hamilton sitting joint-second in the standings, 59 points adrift of Antonelli.

The expected penalty for Antonelli should only serve to increase Ferrari’s chances of fighting for victory at their home race, as they look to make inroads into Mercedes’ 87-point lead in the Constructors’ Championship.

Racing at Monza in front of such a passionate fanbase is always a sight to behold during the year, and if one of Hamilton or Charles Leclerc can deliver a win then the atmosphere underneath the iconic podium will be something particularly special.

Celebrating a legend

Aside from Ferrari’s own hopes of victory, they will be paying tribute to one of the most successful drivers in Formula 1 history this coming weekend.

Michael Schumacher won five of his seven drivers’ titles with Ferrari from 2000-2004, but 2026 marks 30 years since the legendary German joined the team, and 20 years since his final Monza victory for the Scuderia – on the same weekend he announced his first retirement from the sport.

It took five years to taste championship success, but there were still three race wins in his first season in red back in 1996 – including at Monza – as Schumacher secured a victory in each of his 11 seasons with Ferrari.

The team have revealed special race suits that will be worn by Hamilton and Leclerc that feature Schumacher’s logo and the seven stars he used to carry on his helmet design to signify his seven world titles. Ferrari say this week’s tributes are inspired by Schumacher’s “impact on the racing world” and “his enduring mindset”.

title: Vowles admits he worried about losing both Sainz and Albon
excerpt:
James Vowles has admitted that he was concerned by the possibility of Williams losing both Carlos Sainz and Alex Albon amid the team’s struggles this season, and says the confirmation both drivers will be staying on for next year has seen a “weight lifted” off the factory.

The 2025 campaign saw the Grove-based outfit climb from their previous ninth in the championship to an impressive fifth, a run of form that included two podium finishes for Sainz.

Things have proven much more challenging for Williams in 2026, however, with the team back down to P9 after only scoring 11 points so far. Despite the difficulties, both Sainz and Albon were recently confirmed as staying with the squad into next season.

Speaking to the media during the Dutch Grand Prix weekend – days on from the announcements – Vowles was asked whether he had been worried about losing them.

“[I was] concerned about losing both, because they are World Championship-material drivers that deserve the opportunity to be fighting for podiums or more, and we haven't delivered that,” he explained.

“And more than that, we had a scope of where we were moving to. I think that there's no doubt if you sort of look to the outside – I hope there's no doubt – over the last few years, we've been slowly stepping forward with last year being a blip. I think [it was] too positive from where we were, but a step in the right direction.

“So for us to move backwards isn't just a surprise to the drivers, it's a surprise to everyone else, and that will always create risk that you lose them. What I'm thankful for is, the moment we had problems, they stood by our side.

“There wasn't finger pointing, it was actually, ‘tell me what I can do’, and they both came into the factory, spoke to the whole organisation and gave them a lift. Carlos did the same and Alex did the same this week once they re-signed.

“They wanted to make sure that they were here with the team. They want this to be a part of them, that is here on a turnaround of this organisation, and I'm thankful for that. But it's also an indication of what we've shown them in the back end of what's happened and what we're doing about it.”

Albon and Sainz explain why they have kept faith in Williams

Vowles went on to outline why retaining Sainz and Albon was “incredibly important” to him.

“[Reason number] one, it shows the outside world – I can't tell you everything that's going on behind the scenes, but I can tell them, and if they are re-signing it will give you an indication that there's a lot of change ongoing and they believe in what the future looks like.

“And that belief is incredibly important, whether it's for team members or for anyone in the outside world.

“Number two, that consistency is important because the team is really maturing and changing and, as much as you can keep consistent, especially in a driver line-up, it becomes desperately important in order to keep building on that.

“Probably the best way to summarise it to you is [that in] the factory, there's a weight lifted off it this week as the result of it and I've seen them move forward at a much faster pace as a result, so the belief is real and tangible.”

With Albon’s re-signing publicly confirmed first before Sainz’s followed one day later, Vowles also suggested that there was a reason behind the separate announcements.

“For me, and for the drivers, it was important to state that they are different stories and different timings,” the Team Principal said.

“Also, it helped me because Alex was in the simulator on Tuesday and Carlos on Wednesday. I was able to show them to the team and I didn't have them both on the same day at the same time!

“But for me, they're different journeys. Alex has been here since 2022. He has dedicated so much of his life to this project and he wants it to be successful, and I think that's one message in its own right.

“With Carlos, what he needed was to be demonstrated what's happening behind the scenes and he wanted to then commit into the long term, and it's a very different set of arrangements that we have between the two of them. I think the messaging is no different though.

“We all have unfinished business. Our goal is to have Alex and Carlos by our side for many years to come. We have to do work on our side in order to make sure we are stepping up, irrespective of our drivers. The drivers are not the limitation to us at the moment. We are.

“We have to fix that, and quickly, for us more than anything else. But the announcements of the drivers will show you that there's belief in the project for the long term, and that individuals, even the ones that have been here since ‘22, can see the change and want to be a part of it.”

title: F1 NATION: Will Antonelli or Ferrari be home heroes at Monza?
excerpt:
Lando Norris is riding a wave of impressive form having taken back-to-back victories in the last two Grands Prix.

The reigning World Champion claimed wins either side of the Formula 1 summer break at the Hungaroring and then at Zandvoort.

But next up is a very different type of challenge, as the F1 teams and drivers head to Monza for this weekend's Italian Grand Prix.

Will the low downforce Temple of Speed circuit expose McLaren's weaknesses? Or could Norris really turbo-charge his title challenge by making it three wins in a row?

He might be aided in his quest by the fact that championship leader Kimi Antonelli will be taking a grid penalty at his home race, so if the Italian is going to claim a seventh Grand Prix win of the season, he's going to have to fight his way up the order to do it.

The partisan home crowd will of course be cheering on Ferrari, but after going two races without a podium for the first time this season, can the Scuderia find form again and give the Tifosi a race to remember?

And after crashing on the opening lap at his home race last time out, can Max Verstappen bounce back with a strong result at a track where he's won three of the last four Grands Prix?

Tom Clarkson is joined by former Renault F1 driver Jolyon Palmer and IndyCar winner James Hinchcliffe to discuss all that and plenty more in this week's F1 Nation podcast.

The team have a full preview of this weekend's Grand Prix, plus there's reaction to Franco Colapinto extending his contract with Alpine for 2027 – and the team remember when Jolyon upset Fernando Alonso at Monza.

title: What time is the 2026 Italian GP and how can I watch it?
excerpt:
The 2026 Formula 1 season continues this weekend with the Italian Grand Prix, with Monza set to host Round 13 – and here are the global start times for Sunday’s race.

A strong weekend for McLaren’s Lando Norris in the Netherlands indicated that the fight at the top is heating up, with the reigning World Champion clinching back-to-back victories for the first time in 2026. He’s still got a significant deficit to championship leader Kimi Antonelli, who holds a 59-point lead over both his team mate George Russell and Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton.

Head to the RACE HUB or scroll down for more on how and when you can watch the action, along with the global start times for each session.

What time is the 2026 Italian Grand Prix?

The weekend will begin with FP1 on Friday, 4 September at 1230 local time, followed by FP2 at 1600.

A final hour of practice takes place at 1230 on Saturday, 5 September before the drivers compete for the best grid spots in Qualifying at 1600. Lastly, the Grand Prix starts at 1500 on Sunday, 6 September.

Check out the image below to find all the global start times for Sunday’s race.

How can I watch the 2026 Italian Grand Prix?

You can enjoy coverage from every session live on F1 TV Pro (available in selected countries), which brings fans closer to the action via exclusive features like onboard cameras on all 22 of the drivers’ cars, and access to both Pre-Race and Post-Race Shows.

F1 TV Pro can be streamed easily via Apple TV, Chromecast Generation 2 and above, Android TV, Google TV, Amazon Fire TV, and Roku. F1 TV Pro is free of ad breaks and available with commentary in six languages.

Fans can also watch via F1 TV Premium, a premier service that invites fans to step into the heart of the action with the ability to watch races in 4K Ultra HD/HDR on up to six different devices, as well as a personalised Multiview feature available on select devices with 26 different feeds to choose from.

Viewers can watch every F1 Grand Prix, F1 Sprint, Qualifying and practice session live in 4K Ultra HD/HDR at home, with F2, F3, F1 ACADEMY and Porsche Supercup sessions also available to watch live on the platform.

Alternatively, live timing will be available on F1.com and the F1 app across every session during the Grand Prix weekend.

Where is the 2026 Italian Grand Prix taking place?

The Italian Grand Prix will be held at the Autodromo Nazionale Monza, the oldest circuit on the calendar. Originally constructed in 1922, it became the world’s third purpose-built race track and was part of the inaugural F1 season in 1950.

It has hosted nearly every Italian Grand Prix since, with the exception of the 1980 event when the venue underwent refurbishment, and is loved for its history, remarkable high speeds and the passionate Tifosi.

They were delighted by Charles Leclerc's fairytale victories in Monza in 2019 and 2024, but it’s Hamilton and Michael Schumacher who jointly hold the record of five wins.

What is the weather forecast in Italy?

Conditions are expected to be warm and sunny, with temperatures reaching 30 Celsius across all three days of track action and minimal chance of rain in the region.

When can I watch F2 and F3 during the 2026 Dutch Grand Prix weekend?

Formula 2 returns to action this weekend, with Nikola Tsolov seeking to extend his 20-point lead over Gabriele Mini in the championship.

Free Practice will start proceedings at 1000 local time on Friday, September 4, followed by Qualifying at 1455.

The Sprint Race, which sees the top 10 finishers from Qualifying reversed, will take place at 1415 on Saturday, September 5 before the lights go out for the Feature Race at 0945 on Sunday, September 6.

F3 will also contest the penultimate round of the season at Monza as Freddie Slater and Ugo Ugochukwu continue to battle for the title. The weekend will begin with Free Practice at 0855 on Friday, September 4, with the field divided into two groups for Qualifying A at 1400 and Qualifying B at 1420.

The top 12 qualifiers will be reversed for the Sprint Race at 0930 on Saturday, September 5, and the Feature Race will conclude the weekend at 0815 on Sunday, September 6.

title: Kimi Antonelli remains optimistic at Italian GP chances despite 'full thing' penalty
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli remains optimistic of his chances of success in the Italian Grand Prix, despite being set to take a huge grid penalty at his home race.

Antonelli will incur a back-of-the-grid drop at Monza after qualifying, after taking a complete new power unit of the same specification into his pool of parts.

The Italian has already used the maximum four Internal Combustion Engines (ICEs), and three energy stores and control electronics, in addition to four exhausts. He is still within tolerance of the turbocharger and MGU-K, but the decision has been taken to introduce a fully new unit for the title run-in.

Reflecting on that, in front of his home crowd, which means he can win qualifying but will not be starting on pole, Antonelli, who leads the drivers' standings by 59 points from team-mate George Russell and Lewis Hamilton in a points tie for second, was fully on board with the decision.

"Obviously, going into Monza [with the] engine penalty, I still think it’s the best track where to take it to," Antonelli told media, including RacingNews365.

"Of course, it’s my home race and all that kind of stuff, but I think it’s the best race to do so.

"So, I think it still will give me a chance to get a great result and bring home good points."

His boss Toto Wolff had previously spoken how the team's computer simulations had indicated Monza was the "best track" to take the required penalty.

"Our theory, our calculations say that it's the best track to take it," Wolff had said.

"Obviously, algorithms don't consider nationality when we have to fight for a championship and want to get the most PR, so that's what we're going to do."

Drivers are permitted a pool of components for the season, with the Italian driver having used four internal combustion engines, four exhausts, three energy stores (battery) and three control electronics – meaning he’s hit the permitted limits for these components. He still has one allowance for the turbocharger and MGU-K.

title: Sebastian Vettel to make special Ferrari return at Italian GP
excerpt:
Sebastian Vettel will get behind the wheel of a Ferrari car once again at the Italian Grand Prix this weekend, the team has confirmed.

Vettel raced for the Italian squad for six years, winning 14 grands prix for the team - the most behind Michael Schumacher and Niki Lauda.

Schumacher is being honoured by Ferrari at the Italian Grand Prix this weekend with the team introducing a throwback livery as it celebrates the seven-time champion's highly successful 10-year stint.

However, he his being celebrated even further as Vettel, along with Rubens Barrichello, will drive a lap around the track.

Barrichello, a long-time Ferrari team-mate of Schumacher, will get behind the wheel of the F2002 on Saturday around Monza.

Vettel, who has long shared a strong friendship with Schumacher, will have his turn in the same car prior to the start of Sunday's grand prix.

Ferrari has detailed that the car will be operated by its F1 Clienti department and will use an “advanced sustainable fuel developed specifically by Shell, drawing on the know-how acquired this season to create the fuel being used in 2026.”

Three of Schumacher's Ferrari cars will also be on display throughout the weekend at Monza.

They will be the 1996 F310 and the 2006 248 F1, Schumacher's first and last cars with Ferrari, as well as the F2002.

title: Jenson Button details Fernando Alonso hope ahead of ‘difficult’ future decision
excerpt:
2009 F1 champion Jenson Button has detailed that he hopes Fernando Alonso will continue to compete in the sport next year.

The two-time champion has not yet declared whether he will carry on his F1 career with Aston Martin amid its disappointing campaign thus far.

The 2026 challenger from the Silverstone-based squad has been languishing well down the pecking order, with a Honda power unit that has also lacked performance.

Alonso insisted he would use the summer break to reach a decision, but so far is yet to declare his intentions for 2027.

Button, however, who is a former team-mate of Alonso, thinks the 45-year-old still has plenty to offer.

“I retired aged 36, nine years younger than Fernando, but I was ready,” Button said.

“I’d spent a couple of years struggling with racing because I didn’t really want to be there. It felt like there wasn’t anything new for me to achieve and when you get to that point you know it’s time to go.

“But I think the difference for Fernando is there’s still an exciting challenge in front of him.

“Obviously, this year has been tough, but it’s still an exciting time to be at Aston Martin Aramco and to be working with people like Adrian Newey. Any F1 driver would love to race a car designed by him, and to experience firsthand him driving this team forward.”

Alonso has been in this situation before, having opted to walk away from F1 at the end of 2018 to pursue different projects.

However, his next decision to exit the sport will likely be with the understanding that there will be no return again in the future.

“I know how difficult it is to decide your future, and he’s been there once before,” Button added.

“He left the sport and came back, so he obviously left too early. Now, he will make sure that he’s 100 per cent certain that he doesn’t want to be in the sport before he leaves.

“Fernando’s still got so much more to give in F1. I would love to see him in an Aston Martin fighting for wins. That’s where he should be, and it’s where this team is aiming to be. He hasn’t won as much as he should have.

“He’s found himself in unlucky situations a few times, one alongside me, but the talent and hunger is still there, which is the key to staying in the sport and being competitive.”

title: Ferrari unveil Michael Schumacher-inspired livery for Italian Grand Prix
excerpt:
Scuderia Ferrari has confirmed a special tribute livery for the Italian Grand Prix this weekend, dedicated to Michael Schumacher's extraordinary decade with the team.

The Maranello outfit has revealed a Schumacher-inspired design for its SF-26, alongside bespoke race suits for Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton that underline the theme, which were launched last week.

The overalls feature white striping down the front and across the shoulders, Schumacher's personal logo, and seven white stars on the back representing his seven world titles.

The tribute is timed to mark 30 years since Schumacher's first Ferrari victory in 1996 and 20 years since his final season with the team in 2006.

Across that remarkable spell, the German won 72 grands prix and five consecutive drivers' championships from 2000 to 2004, transforming Ferrari into the most dominant force the sport had ever seen.

The SF-26 livery features a completely red design, getting rid of the white engine cover that has been used since the start of the year.

The font of the numbers is also a throwback to Ferrari during Schumacher's era, with the seven-time champion's signature also incorporated into the design.

title: Theft sparks police investigation at new Spanish GP F1 venue
excerpt:
A police investigation has been launched following allegations of thieves stealing electrical wiring and cables from the new host venue of F1's Spanish Grand Prix.

The Madring in Madrid will host its first race over the weekend of September 11th-13th, after the Spanish Grand Prix moved from Barcelona for 2026.

With just two weeks to go before the race, reputable Spanish outlet ABC has reported that police are investigating the theft of around 300m of electrical cabling and wiring from the circuit, which is located in the IFEMA entertainment complex near Real Madrid's training complex and Barajas airport.

It is understood that the affected areas of the track came through a tunnel, which would indicate Turns 17 and 18 as the location of the theft, although back-up and contingency plans are in place.

FIA F3 recently held a test day at the venue ahead of its championship finale on the F1 support bill, with F1 cars having already run at the track, with Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc completing a filming day earlier this year.

title: Lewis Hamilton rescues 'car of dreams' from barn in stunning overhaul
excerpt:
Check out the project Lewis Hamilton has been working on with Ferrari...

title: Red Bull 'narrative' questioned after high-profile exits
excerpt:
Former F1 driver David Coulthard has questiond the narrative surrounding Red Bull following a number of big name departures in recent years.

Many of the senior staff members that were part of the squad during its successful years with Sebastian Vettel and Max Verstappen, respectively, have moved on.

These names include Christian Horner, Helmut Marko, Adrian Newey, Jonathan Wheatley, Rob Marshall and Gianpiero Lambiase, with the latter set to join McLaren in 2028.

However, Verstappen himself has insisted on several ocassions that they are just a few names of the some 1,200 employees that contribute to Red Bull's success.

It's a remark that Coulthard mirrored, pointing to the huge hiring process the team took on when it set up its engine facility for its 2026 entry.

“I was talking to someone at Red Bull a few weeks ago about this,” Coulthard told the Up to Speed podcast.

“The reality is they came up with a number that the amount of people that had left versus the amount of people who joined from Ferrari, Mercedes, the rivals, was in favour of people coming in.

“If you look at [Red Bull] Powertrains, they basically started from scratch, built a factory and hired a few hundred people.

“Those few hundred people weren’t coming from motorbikes and all the rest of it - they were coming from other F1 teams.

“It’s one of those things where the narrative suited the ‘poker finger, the wheels have come off the wagon’-type scenario. But it’s constantly happening.

“All of the teams are hiring and firing, people on gardening leave and what have you.”

Verstappen has comitted his future to Red Bull, recently penning an extension that will see him remain at the team until at least the 2030 season.

The Dutchman has praised the impact of team boss Laurent Mekies, with Coulthard telling RacingNews365 that it's clear the two share a harmonious relationship.

While Coulthard admitted some major names have left the team, he stated a single figure can no longer directly impact the form of an outfit.

“So I don’t see anything unique in that at all because yes, Adrian and people like that are headline names and they have clearly captained the ships very well.

“But the sport now has become so complex, not one person can make it the deciding factor.”

title: Toto Wolff is 'absolutely conscious' of emerging threat to Mercedes F1 titles
excerpt:
Toto Wolff says he is "absolutely conscious" of Mercedes falling foul of a Max Verstappen-style comeback in the 2026 title race amid McLaren's resurgence.

Although Kimi Antonelli leads the drivers' standings by 59 points from George Russell and Lewis Hamilton of Ferrari, and 83 from the McLaren of Lando Norris, the reigning champions emerged from the races in Hungary and the Netherlands with two wins and renewed hope of reeling in Antonelli and Mercedes to defend their crowns.

In 2025, Verstappen of Red Bull found himself 104 points behind Oscar Piastri after the Dutch GP, but embarked on a stunning end to the season, and overhauled the Australian, but ultimately fell just two points short of stealing the drivers' title from Norris.

After the Zandvoort race, Wolff explained that Mercedes simply did not 'have the money' to spend on upgrades at the rate of McLaren or Ferrari, with the team operating within the "financial realities" of the cost cap, with the last big upgrade being delivered at the Canadian GP in May.

In the constructors' standings, Mercedes leads Ferrari by 87 points and McLaren by 162, with Wolff addressing the prospect of a Verstappen-style comeback from Norris in the drivers' fight.

"Yeah, I mean, absolutely conscious of the fact, but it is not only Norris, but we also have a [59]-point gap to Lewis," Wolff told media, including RacingNews365, when asked about the renewed threat posed by McLaren.

"That's something you need to be worried about, so it is going to be tough, and it could become tighter.

"We just need to do the optimum job every single weekend, every single session, every single weekend.

"We have opposition that is good enough to win races, and they've done two now on tracks where they've been very, very good in the previous years also, so let's see if we can regain some momentum."

title: Ferrari unable to deliver every Lewis Hamilton demand after 'shake-up' arrival
excerpt:
Ferrari boss Fred Vasseur has explained that he was not able to meet all of Lewis Hamilton's demands about how to fix the team.

Hamilton said earlier this year that Vasseur had "moved mountains" in making changes the seven-time champion had requested ahead of 2026 following his poor 2025 season.

It later emerged that one of these changes concerned the brake system of the Ferrari car, with Hamilton requesting the use of Carbon Industrie brake discs rather than the Brembo materials Ferrari has long used in its partnership with the firm.

Throughout his tough first season, feeling on the brakes was one of Hamilton's major bugbears, but from the Japanese GP in March, Hamilton was able to use the CI material he had become accustomed to during his success-laden spell with Mercedes, where he took 84 wins and six of his seven titles in a 12-year stay.

Team-mate Charles Leclerc soon followed Hamilton's brake set-up after tough races in Canada and Monaco, but Vasseur has explained that every demand made of him by the drivers, including Hamilton, he cannot make happen.

"Yes, but we didn't do everything that he wanted," Vasseur told Autosport when asked if he had been able to follow every demand Hamilton had requested.

"But suggestions are always welcome. That's true for Lewis; it's true for Charles. It's true for every single driver. After every single event, they are coming with a list of things that they would like to improve.

"On this list, some are out of scope, because you can't do this for the team, and they can understand very quickly that, from a team perspective, it makes no sense for the cost cap or whatever it is.

"Sometimes they don't have the full vision of the situation, but at least it's good for me to understand where they feel we are weak.

"Sometimes with their input you understand something because you were focused on the team vision, and you understand that for the drivers it's a bit different."

Turning to Hamilton's arrival and the championship-winning knowledge he brought with him from Mercedes, Vasseur felt it was "good to shake the system."

"It's good to shake the system a little bit." he said.

"If you stay in your bubble all your life with the same people, at one stage you will struggle to improve. It's true for the drivers. It's true for the engineers when you recruit people from other teams.

"One of the key qualities of drivers is to be able to contribute to the development of the team. The worst-case scenario is that when you start the discussion and you have the feeling that the other is trying to find an excuse, but when you have a good relationship, it's never an excuse.

"I think we have this positive attitude to help each other and to understand that the other can have a different view.

"I'm not always right. I'm not always wrong, and it's only by collaboration, discussion, and exchange that we will improve."

title: Liam Lawson highlights significant Red Bull 'knife-edge' difference
excerpt:
Liam Lawson has explained the significant difference he endured this time around at Red Bull compared to his stint at the start of 2025.

The New Zealander's promotion last year ended after just two rounds as disappointing performances saw him shipped back to the sister Racing Bulls team.

However, his services were required once again last time out at Zandvoort due to an injury for Isack Hadjar.

On this occasion, he impressed as he lapped close to the times set by Max Verstappen before bringing home points in seventh place.

It was a stark contrast to his experience last year - but as Lawson explained, the circumstances were much different.

“The main thing last year was there were two tracks I'd never been to,” Lawson told media including RacingNews365.

“So on top of that, trying to learn a car that was already very hard to drive.

“This car potentially is not so difficult to drive, or difficult to be on the limit.

“So it's more putting everything else together, tyre prep, just getting the balance right in the car and getting used to how it actually drives, versus a car last year that was just very tough to put on the limit.”

“I went into last year, thought I was going to have more time in the car, so I was more or less just adapting to everything that Max had in the car.

“And there's a lot of stuff, just like pedals, steering, everything like that-that was different for me. I didn't have time to get used to it.

“[At Zandvoort], I said let's make it as close to my car as possible.”

Red Bull's car last year was notoriously tricky to drive, with Lawson's replacement Yuki Tsunoda also struggling to extract performance.

But with a new cycle of regulations underway, Lawson asserted it is a much different challenger to drive this time around.

“Last year the car was on such a knife edge, at least at the start, that if you weren't on that limit, then it was a huge lap time killer,” he said.

“This year there are so many more factors in there.

“Having more time in this car and this regulation period, as much as the car is very, very different, there are a lot of things that factor into putting a lap together with these power units. Having the same power unit helps as well.”

title: Oscar Piastri prepared for 'different beast' battle in McLaren waiting game
excerpt:
Oscar Piastri is prepared for a "different beast" battle at Monza as McLaren will discover whether its strong F1 form will translate at the Italian Grand Prix.

Piastri's team-mate Lando Norris has taken pole and won both races on the immediate side of the summer break in Hungary and the Netherlands, with these circuits dominated by short straights and a lot of long corners.

In contrast, Monza is the fastest circuit in F1, with the records for fastest pole lap and fastest elapsed race time being broken in 2025, albeit in the final year of the ground effect regulations.

However, McLaren has been open that its MCL40 chassis is draggy, a trait which is not suited to Monza, with the nascent talk of the team's title comeback charge set for its first examination this coming weekend.

"I mean, it's difficult to know because these two circuits are quite similar in characteristics: very short straights, a lot of corners, and generally quite long corners," Piastri said to media, including RacingNews365, about the Hungaroring and Zandvoort when looking ahead to how McLaren would fare at Monza.

"Monza is going to be a completely different beast for a number of reasons, but we'll have to wait and see if this pace translates to other circuits."

Offering further details about his ongoing struggles with the car, Piastri explained how he is just lacking pace.

"I think in the races, the rear of the car is very tricky to drive, and even in qualifying, the last few weekends it's been difficult, but [the Dutch GP] weekend in qualifying was much nicer, and I felt much more confident," he said.

"And I think at certain points of the race, I felt a lot better with that, but it is just that the pace hasn't been there.

"It's not the first race this year that that's been the case. Some have been good, some have been very strong, but there have been too many now that have been really a long way

off."

title: Jenson Button escapes unscathed from frightening Monza crash with Honda - On This Day
excerpt:
20 years ago, on this day in 2006, Jenson Button escaped injury after a serious accident during a test day at the Monza circuit.

20 years ago today, Jenson Button suffered one of the biggest accidents of his F1 career during a test at Monza.

Among the famous corners at the Italian track is the final corner, commonly referred to as the 'Parabolica', where cars travel at approximately 260 kilometres per hour.

The speed is often augmented due to the low-downforce configuration that teams use to prepare for the race at Monza.

According to initial reports, Button’s crash was caused by a problem with the left rear, presumably involving the suspension or wheel mounting.

Button braked for the turn and turned the wheel, after which the rear of the car suddenly lost traction. The RA106 shot straight into the gravel trap, skidded across the gravel at high speed, and then crashed hard into the tyre barriers.

The impact caused significant damage. The left side of the car, in particular, was severely damaged along nearly its entire length, while parts of the suspension and bodywork were also lost.

© xpb.cc

© xpb.cc

Honda breathes a sigh of relief

Despite the force of the impact, the cockpit remained intact.

Button was able to climb out of the car on his own and immediately reported that he had not sustained any injuries.

Honda breathed a sigh of relief, although the crash did cause a significant interruption to the test programme.

The test at Monza was focused on preparing for the fast Italian circuit, where engine power, stability under braking, and efficient aerodynamic setup are crucial.

Afterwards, the team investigated the cause of the failure to prevent a recurrence during the grand prix weekend.

title: Red Bull detail additional benefit to Max Verstappen extension
excerpt:
Red Bull team principal Laurent Mekies has detailed an additional benefit to the extension of Max Verstappen's contract with the team.

The four-time world champion committed his long-term future to Red Bull earlier this year, signing an extension that will keep him at Milton Keynes until the end of 2030.

Red Bull has seen notable personnel departures in recent seasons, with key figures moving on to rival outfits.

However, Mekies believes Verstappen's presence now serves as a powerful magnet, one that could attract top engineering and technical talent to the organisation.

"It's massively important," Mekies told media including RacingNews365. "You know the good guys, and at the end of the day, you are only interested in the good guys and girls.

"The good guys, they have the choice and I'm talking about our people, and I'm talking about the people in other teams, they have the choice because they are very, very good at what they do.

"And as much as Max had to choose which team to commit to, they have the choice to commit left or right, and we are all united by only one thing, we want to win.

"And when you're able to say that the fastest driver in the world is with us, it's a massive stability element. It's a massive ambition element."

Red Bull has endured a difficult start to the 2026 campaign, but Mekies stressed the team remains singularly focused on returning to the front of the grid.

"Then everybody understands that everything else that you set up is only with that single objective, to win,” he said. “So it's a very big element.

"We must not use that as an excuse. So it's a very big plus. We need to work on everything else to make sure that we keep developing and attracting all the talents."
